Power management in CPU architectures relies on dynamic frequency and voltage scaling,  where lower frequencies and voltages are used for light computations and higher ones for intense tasks.  However, building efficient hardware for such a scheme is challenging and largely unexplored in the field of computer architecture.  In this work, we present a new CPU architecture called HyperDegrade, which utilizes two operating modes beyond the typical frequency-voltage spectrum.  In a test with real-world workloads, HyperDegrade showed a 30% improvement in energy efficiency compared to the state-of-the-art architecture, a 3.5-fold reduction in average frequency, and a 2.5-fold increase in average performance per cycle.  Additionally, HyperDegrade outperformed several existing designs in performance and efficiency in benchmark tests.  The design was further validated through a TSMC 16nm prototype, which demonstrated a 2.5-fold boost in performance at the same power consumption as the Braille architecture, a 4.5-fold boost in performance at the same area as Braille, and a 20% reduction in power consumption for a given performance compared to Braille.  Our research provides a novel approach to designing CPU architectures, which can be highly efficient through the use of multiple operating modes and eliminates the need for active feedback mechanisms and performance monitoring units.  The design can also be production-ready with minimal additional cost.  The HyperDegrade architecture and its derivatives offer significant implications for the design of future low-power CPU architectures.  The code and schematics of the design are available for public use on GitHub. He presented two questions concerning the equivalency of certain metrics in these spaces at a math conference in Paris. Although his questions have been published, reliable information on their status is hard to find. He even went so far as to restate them in English in 1940, with the intention of rewarding a $50 bonus to whoever could solve them. Initially, these problems seemed significant, but as the field of mathematics evolved, Menger decreased the bonus to just $25, deeming the questions less important. Moreover, we also derive a more general solution applicable to a broader class of distance defining functions within these spaces. Finally, we believe that our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of these spaces and their properties, laying the groundwork for further research and exploration.
